titre: The 1.375 frame of talking pictures is what the soundtrack left to the image
accroche: Since 1932, the image of a studio film has measured 0.825 by 0.600 inch: a ratio of 1.375, not 4:3. Sound trimmed the silent-era image.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 9, 1932, at the Washington convention, the Society of Motion Picture Engineers (SMPE) adopts two dimensions for 35 mm film: a projector aperture 0.600 inch high by 0.825 wide, and a camera aperture of 0.631 by 0.868. Divide the width by the height: 0.825 over 0.600 gives 1.375. That isn't 4:3, which is 1.33. It will be called the Academy ratio, and it will be used, according to Wikipedia, for 35 mm studio films from 1932 to 1952.

To understand this small difference, we have to go back to silent film. In a January 1930 article in the Journal of the SMPE, Loyd A. Jones, of Kodak, recalls that the very first films had width-to-height ratios ranging from 1.25 to 2.0, before practice settled on a rectangle of four units by three. The standard silent projection aperture measured about 0.906 by 0.680 inch: a ratio of 1.33, the image taking up the full width between the two rows of perforations.

## Sound takes its place

With talkies, a photographed soundtrack has to fit on the same film, between the image and the perforations. Jones puts it bluntly: sound requires shrinking the available image area. In the same issue, Lester Cowan, of the Academy, gives the so-called Movietone aperture as about 0.820 wide by 0.680 high, a ratio of 1.2. Theaters cope each in their own way. A survey of August 9, 1929, carried out for the Academy by the firm Electrical Research Products in 306 theaters west of Denver, finds four different methods there. One consists of reducing the aperture to 0.600 by 0.800 to recover the 1.33 on a smaller area.

The 1932 dimensions put an end to this disorder. The Progress Committee report, in the same volume of the Journal (August 1932), adds that the soundtrack measures 0.100 inch wide, with a black band of 0.017 inch between the image and the track, and 0.004 between the track and the perforations. The 1.375 ratio is the quotient of the two dimensions of the projector aperture, whose 0.600 height is that of the reduced apertures. The same report states that standardization will remove the most vexing difficulties that studios and theaters have met since the arrival of sound.

## What this shifts

From the published dimensions, a simple calculation shows the price of this arrangement: 0.825 times 0.600 gives about 0.495 square inch, against about 0.616 for the silent aperture (0.906 times 0.680). The talking-picture image therefore occupies roughly a fifth less area on the same film.

The “old square format” is often presented as the natural shape of cinema, that of the screen before widescreen arrived. But the 1.33 rectangle is itself an early choice, among other ratios tried. And the talkie frame is not that rectangle: it is what was left of the film once room had been made for a strip of sound. A supposedly natural image shape bears the trace of everything that had to be fitted in beside it.

repere.texte: On May 9, 1932, the SMPE adopts for 35 mm a projector aperture of 0.600 by 0.825 inch and a camera aperture of 0.631 by 0.868. The projector ratio is 1.375, not 1.33 as in silent film.
repere.source: Journal of the SMPE, vol. 19, 1932, “New Dimensional Standards,” p. 924

carte.punch: The 1932 film format isn't 4:3: it's 1.375, after sound trimmed the image.
carte.idee: In 1932, the SMPE sets the 35 mm projection aperture at 0.825 by 0.600 inch, a ratio of 1.375. Silent film was at 1.33 across the full width of the film: the soundtrack took up room, and the talkie frame is what was left.

quiz.question: Why does the image lose width on the film stock with the arrival of talkies, before the 1932 standard?
choix: Because the first equipped theaters wanted to copy the shape of television screens
Because the photographed soundtrack takes up a strip of the film, which reduces the width available for the image
Because 35 mm is replaced by a narrower film stock in sound theaters
Because the Academy imposes a wider frame so that actors look bigger
quiz.explication: Sound is photographed on the film, between the image and the perforations, and takes up one hundred thousandths of an inch of width. The film stays 35 mm, the Academy isn't trying to enlarge the actors, and television is not yet a model for theaters: the image is simply reduced, then standardized at 1.375 in 1932.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which organization adopts the new 35 mm film dimensions on May 9, 1932, at the Washington convention?
choix: The Society of Motion Picture Engineers (SMPE)
The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the Society of Motion Picture Engineers that adopts, on May 9, 1932, at the Washington convention, the projector aperture of 0.600 by 0.825 inch and the camera aperture of 0.631 by 0.868, as the entry says.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many different methods did the survey carried out for the Academy in 306 theaters west of Denver record?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The survey of August 9, 1929, carried out by Electrical Research Products for the Academy in 306 theaters west of Denver, finds four different methods used by theaters to adapt to the arrival of sound, according to the entry.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the calculation presented in the entry, how much image area does the Academy format lose compared with the silent-film aperture, on the same film stock?
choix: No loss, the two apertures have the same area
About a tenth of the area
About a fifth of the area
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The calculation gives about 0.495 square inch for the 1932 aperture against about 0.616 for the silent one, roughly a fifth less area, as the entry indicates.
